headline: Home Depot: sales up 4.9% and comps positive, but full-year earnings growth is guided to about 2%
takeaway: Sales rose 4.9% to $43.4 billion with comparable sales up 2.2%, and adjusted EPS of $3.86 was just ahead of the $3.84 consensus. The incoming chief executive said results exceeded expectations, yet the updated guidance points to adjusted earnings growth of only about 2% for the year, and the shares fell 2.5%.
results: Home Depot reported third-quarter sales of $43.4 billion, up $2.0 billion or 4.9% from a year earlier. Comparable sales increased 2.2%, both in total and in the United States. Adjusted diluted earnings per share were $3.86 against $3.74 a year ago and a consensus of about $3.84; reported EPS was $3.72 against $3.62.

Net earnings were $3.7 billion compared with $3.6 billion. The gap between total sales growth of 4.9% and comparable growth of 2.2% reflects new stores and the contribution of acquired distribution businesses, which add revenue without adding to the comparable-store figure.
At quarter end the company operated 2,372 stores and more than 1,320 SRS locations, the specialty distribution business it bought to serve professional contractors.
mgmt: Richard McPhail, the incoming chief executive, said third-quarter results exceeded the company’s expectations and credited execution and continued investment for market share gains in what he called a dynamic environment. Ann-Marie Campbell, the incoming president and chief operating officer, was quoted alongside him — the release itself marks a leadership transition.

The company updated its fiscal 2026 guidance to total sales growth of approximately 4.5%, comparable sales growth of approximately 1.4%, a gross margin of approximately 33.0% and an adjusted operating margin of approximately 12.8%. Adjusted diluted EPS is expected to grow approximately 2.0% from $14.69, and reported EPS approximately 1.5% from $14.23.
It expects to open approximately 15 new stores and to spend about 2.5% of sales on capital expenditure, with net interest expense of about $2.2 billion.
view: Home Depot is a housing-turnover business waiting for housing to turn over, and this quarter shows a company executing well against a market that has not yet recovered. A comparable sales increase of 2.2% is a real improvement on the declines of the last two years, and it is still a long way from the mid-single-digit growth this business produces when people are moving house. Homeowners locked into cheap mortgages do not move, and people who do not move do not undertake large renovation projects — which is where Home Depot earns the most.

The guidance tells you how management reads the next few months, and the reading is cautious. Full-year comparable growth of about 1.4% and adjusted EPS growth of about 2% is a muted outlook from a company that just reported a quarter ahead of its own expectations. That combination — a beat alongside a modest guide — is why the shares fell. The market wanted evidence that the recovery was accelerating and received evidence that it is stabilising.

The strategic shift toward professional contractors deserves more attention than the comp. The 1,320 SRS locations are a distribution business selling roofing, landscaping and pool supplies to trade customers, a different customer and a different margin structure from the orange-box store. It is why total sales grew 4.9% while comps grew 2.2%, and it is why the operating margin guide of 12.8% sits below where Home Depot used to run: distribution earns less per dollar of sales than retail. The trade-off is a larger addressable market in exchange for a structurally lower margin.

Net interest expense of $2.2 billion is the cost of having bought that business with debt, and it is the reason earnings growth trails sales growth. When housing turnover returns — and deferred maintenance on an ageing housing stock makes it a question of when — Home Depot has operating leverage in both the stores and the distribution network. Until then this is a high-quality franchise growing earnings at about 2% on a multiple that expects more. The leadership transition adds a variable, though the incoming chief executive was the finance chief and the strategy is unlikely to change.
watch: Comparable transactions against average ticket, and big-ticket project sales. Larger projects coming back is the first sign that housing turnover is recovering; small-ticket maintenance holding up is merely the business being resilient.
